title: Truth's letters
hookLine: alef, mem, tav: some teachers say remove the alef and it becomes met, dead

cards: What's the distance between true and dead? In Hebrew, one letter. The word for truth is emet: alef, mem, tav.
Put your thumb over the alef and two letters are left: met. Dead. Some teachers have built a whole lesson on that missing letter.

A later legend even turns it into a story: a clay figure, a golem, comes alive when emet is written on its forehead, and stops when someone erases the alef. That's a legend, told and retold, not scripture.
But the question it points at is a real one.

teach.b: Emet. Truth. Four ways into it.
Alef opens the alef-bet, tav closes it, and mem stands near the middle.

The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says the seal of the Holy One is emet, the seal from earlier this year, and some readers notice that the word reaches from the first letter, through the center, to the last.
Truth, on that reading, runs from beginning to end. Second, the alef. It makes no sound of its own; you can read the word aloud and barely notice it.
Some teachers read that silent first letter as a sign of the One, God, at the head of every true thing. Take it away and what's left is met.
Their lesson: words can be accurate and still lifeless, if the first thing is missing. Third, the text.
The prophet Zechariah says: "Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour."
Truth here is said to someone, face to face.
And a psalm says: "The LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth." In truth means more than correct facts. It means meaning what you say.
Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. Plenty of dead truths aren't lies. They're facts with the alef taken off: correct and cold, or missing the part that would change the picture.
Keep the first letter, the teachers say, and the words stay alive.

how: Jewish teachers cite the Talmud's line that God's seal is truth, and the closing words of the Shema in the prayer book run straight into the word emet.

o: an oath, the words you swear in a court
truth, spelled from the first letter to the last
a seal, the stamp pressed into wax on a letter

p: the first letter, and it's silent
what's left without the alef: dead

s: emet and met differ by one letter
take the alef off emet, and mem, tav reads met, dead.
the golem story comes from the Torah
it's a later legend. the teaching about the alef comes from teachers, not scripture.
the Talmud calls truth the seal of the Holy One
tractate Shabbat says God's seal is emet.

games.q: a friend asks what you thought of the speech they just gave. it ran long, and one story in it was beautiful. what do you say?
o: "the story about your father was beautiful. it ran long around it."
games.why: on the teachers' reading, the first answer is accurate but missing its alef, and the second isn't true at all. the third keeps both the facts and the care.

practice: Bring to mind something true you need to say to someone soon: hard news, a correction, or just how a thing went.
Say it to yourself the way it first comes out, then ask whether the alef is there: the care, the reason it matters, the part you'd rather leave out.
Shape it again in one sentence, nothing false added and nothing living taken away; if you pray, you can bring that sentence with you when you pray.

wordCard.voice: Emet. Truth: alef, mem, tav, from the first letter to the last. Without its alef, it reads met. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: truth; spelled alef, mem, tav. Without the alef, מֵת, met, dead.

carryVoice: Your line: truth needs the one. Accurate is where truth starts, not where it ends. Until tomorrow.
